mcqs.question: A stakeholder suggests "just redesigning" a live production system from scratch. What does this proposal quietly assume that's usually false at real scale?
options: That the new architecture will be simpler than the old one
That the team has enough headcount to finish the work
That the database schema is already well normalized
That the old system can be frozen and cut over to the new one atomically, with no coexistence period
mcqs.explanation: "Just redesign it" usually hides an assumption that migration can be instant and clean, when in reality the old and new systems must coexist for weeks or months while callers move over. Simplicity, headcount, and schema normalization aren't the core hidden assumption here.

mcqs.question: In an expand-contract migration, what is the key property of the "expand" stage?
options: The new shape is added alongside the old one, with nothing removed, so the system stays fully working at every point
The old shape is immediately deleted to force all callers to switch
All callers are switched to the new shape simultaneously
Data is moved to the new store but the old store is left permanently in place
mcqs.explanation: Expand means adding the new shape without touching the old one, so the system remains valid and working at every step — you could pause for a week and nothing breaks. Deleting the old shape is the contract stage, not expand, and simultaneous cutover contradicts the whole point of the pattern.

mcqs.question: During a dual-write migration, a write to the old store succeeds but the corresponding write to the new store times out. What's the real risk here?
options: The application will crash immediately on the next request
The two stores now silently disagree, and without reconciliation nothing detects the drift before cutover
The old store will automatically roll back its write to match
This is not a real risk since dual-writes are always atomic across two stores
mcqs.explanation: Dual-writes to two separate stores are not atomic, so a partial failure leaves them silently inconsistent, and that drift compounds unless a reconciliation job actively diffs the two stores on a schedule. There's no automatic rollback, and the app doesn't necessarily crash.

mcqs.question: A migration has a hard vendor-contract deadline in two weeks, the system is small, and the new path has been fully tested end to end. Which approach fits best per this topic's guidance?
options: Incremental migration only, regardless of the deadline
Neither approach — wait for the contract to be renegotiated
Big-bang cutover, since it fits a small system with a hard deadline and thorough pre-testing
Dual-writes indefinitely with no eventual cutover
mcqs.explanation: Big-bang cutover is the right fit precisely for small systems with a hard deadline and solid pre-testing — the scenario the topic names as its best case. Incremental migration is the safer default at real scale, but this scenario's constraints favor big-bang, and indefinite dual-writes without a cutover isn't a completed migration at all.

mcqs.question: A team says a migration is "done" because the new system is live and taking traffic. Per this topic, what's missing from that claim?
options: A load test proving the new system can handle peak traffic
Approval from the original design doc's reviewers
A rollback plan in case the new system fails later
A measurable, monitored completion condition — such as zero writes to the old table for 30 days — before contracting the old path
mcqs.explanation: "Live" isn't "done": without a defined, monitored condition for completion, the old path often keeps receiving a trickle of traffic indefinitely from forgotten callers. A load test, doc approval, and a rollback plan are all reasonable practices but don't address this specific gap.
